paragraphs: The Senate had passed the amendment in April 1864, but it stalled in the House until Lincoln pushed for a second vote after his re-election. On 31 January 1865 it cleared the House 119 to 56, a margin so tight it needed several Democrats to cross the aisle, and the chamber erupted when the result was read.

Ratification followed within the year: the required twenty-seven of thirty-six states approved it by 6 December 1865, and it was proclaimed law twelve days later. It abolished slavery and involuntary servitude nationwide except as punishment for crime, a clause still argued over in prison labour cases today.

When the amendment was ratified on 23 January 1964, five states still charged a tax at the ballot box for federal elections: Alabama, Arkansas, Mississippi, Texas and Virginia. The fee itself was often small, but registrars paired it with literacy tests and other hurdles that fell almost entirely on poor and Black voters.

The amendment's reach stopped at federal races; it said nothing about state and local elections, where several of those states kept charging the tax. It took a Supreme Court ruling two years later, Harper v. Virginia State Board of Elections in 1966, to strike poll taxes down everywhere else on equal protection grounds.

The revolt that ended Umayyad rule in 750 was not led by an Abbasid at all. Abu Muslim, a commander of uncertain origins operating out of Khurasan in what is now northeastern Iran, raised an army under the black banner and marched west, defeating the last Umayyad caliph at the Battle of the Zab.

The Abbasid family took the throne Abu Muslim had won for them and, within a few years, had him killed as a threat to their own authority. Their capital did not move to Baghdad immediately either: the caliph al-Mansur founded that city in 762, twelve years after the dynasty itself began.

Scotland came to the table poor. A failed colonial venture on the isthmus of Panama, the Darien scheme, had swallowed roughly 150,000 pounds of Scottish investment, and England had just barred Scottish exports under the 1705 Alien Act unless Edinburgh negotiated union. Scotland's Parliament had also threatened, in 1704, to pick a different monarch than England's chosen Hanoverian heir.

Union came with a price tag: a payment of about 398,000 pounds, called the Equivalent, covered Scotland's share of a joint national debt and reimbursed Darien's investors, while pensions and offices went to peers and MPs whose votes carried the Act. From May 1707 the two parliaments became one, sitting at Westminster under Queen Anne, and Great Britain existed as a single kingdom for the first time.

Four men led the meeting in Bloemfontein on 8 January 1912: lawyer Pixley ka Isaka Seme, writer Sol Plaatje, minister John Dube and Walter Rubusana. All came from South Africa's small class of educated, mission-schooled professionals, and their new congress drew together chiefs and delegates from across the country's Black communities.

Its early strategy was petitioning colonial and imperial authorities rather than confrontation. That shifted around 1920, when the organisation, renamed the African National Congress in 1923, turned to passive resistance campaigns against pass laws that controlled where Black South Africans could live and travel.

Joachim von Ribbentrop and the Japanese ambassador Kintomo Mushanokoji signed the pact in Berlin on 25 November 1936, naming the Communist International as the shared enemy. A secret protocol attached to it was aimed more narrowly at the Soviet Union, committing each side to consult if the other were attacked by Moscow and to avoid agreements that would help the USSR.

Italy joined the following year, turning a bilateral deal into the outline of what would become the Axis, and Spain and Hungary signed on in 1939. During the war itself Finland, Romania, Bulgaria, Slovakia, Croatia and the Japanese-backed Nanjing government all acceded, by which point membership had become less an anti-communist pledge than a declaration of allegiance to Berlin and Tokyo.

Two years before anyone landed on it, the moon already had legal protection. The Outer Space Treaty was opened for signature on 27 January 1967 in London, Moscow and Washington simultaneously, and entered into force that October, months before any crewed mission left Earth orbit.

Its core clauses bar signatories from placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit or on any celestial body, and they forbid any state from claiming sovereignty over the moon or planets by occupation or use. The framework has held for decades without a major violation, even as more nations gained the means to launch.

Congress drafted the Articles while still fighting the Revolutionary War, finishing in November 1777, but getting all thirteen states to ratify took more than three years. Maryland held out longest over western land claims and did not sign until February 1781, just months before Yorktown ended the fighting the confederation had been formed to manage.

The document it produced deliberately kept the new central government weak. Congress could ask states for money but not tax anyone directly, could not regulate trade between states, and any amendment needed every single state's consent. Those gaps left Congress unable to pay its own soldiers reliably and pushed delegates toward the Constitutional Convention six years later.

Cold War anxiety, not economic ambition, brought five foreign ministers to Bangkok's Saranrom Palace on 8 August 1967. Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand signed a short declaration meant partly to keep communist influence and outside powers from filling any vacuum in the region.

The Bangkok Declaration committed the five to accelerate economic, social and cultural cooperation and to settle disputes peacefully among themselves. What began as a loose grouping without a headquarters, budget or binding legal structure grew over the following decades into a bloc that now includes ten Southeast Asian states.

Cleisthenes did not come to power as a reformer. He lost a factional fight to Isagoras, who called in a Spartan army to expel him, then tried to dissolve Athens's governing council. Ordinary citizens resisted, besieged Isagoras and his Spartan backers on the Acropolis, and forced them out, which is how Cleisthenes returned and got the chance to redesign the constitution.

His main change broke the power of the old aristocratic clans: he replaced four family-based tribes with ten new ones grouped by residence, mixing citizens from coast, city and inland into each. He expanded the governing council to five hundred members chosen by lot, and introduced ostracism, a vote that could exile a citizen for ten years without trial.

Roosevelt and Churchill met aboard warships in Placentia Bay, off Newfoundland, in the second week of August 1941, four months before the United States entered the war. What emerged on 14 August was not a treaty either man signed but a jointly telegraphed statement of principles, drafted and redrafted between London and Washington rather than put on paper in one room.

It renounced territorial gain for either country, backed the right of peoples to choose their own government, and called for freed trade, disarmed aggressors and, eventually, a world free of want and fear. Roosevelt would later admit no signed copy of the charter existed anywhere, yet its language shaped the later Declaration by United Nations and the postwar order that followed it.

The alliance that became the Aztec Empire was born out of a succession dispute, not a plan for conquest. When the Tepanec ruler Tezozomoc died in 1426, his heir Maxtla seized power and turned on his own allies, blockading Tenochtitlan and demanding heavier tribute from neighbouring cities. Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan answered by going to war against his capital, Azcapotzalco, and won in 1428.

Two years later the three victors formalised their partnership as the Triple Alliance, agreeing to share the spoils of future conquests, two shares to Tenochtitlan and Texcoco and one to Tlacopan. On paper the three cities remained equals. In practice Tenochtitlan's own armies grew so dominant that within decades it was the alliance in all but name.

Indonesia, Burma, India, Ceylon and Pakistan called the meeting that opened in Bandung on 18 April 1955, and twenty-nine governments sent delegates, together speaking for well over half the world's population. None were the Soviet Union or the United States. Zhou Enlai attended for China and struck a deliberately conciliatory tone, easing fears among smaller delegations about Chinese ambitions in the region.

Delegates left with the Bandung Declaration, ten principles on peaceful coexistence and respect for sovereignty that were aimed squarely at colonial rule and at pressure from both Cold War blocs. Indonesia's Sukarno spoke of a bloc of what he called newly emerging forces. The gathering fed directly into the founding of the Non-Aligned Movement six years later.

The government needed 1.2 million pounds to rebuild a navy the French had beaten in 1690, and it had neither the cash nor the credit to borrow it outright. The Scottish trader William Paterson proposed a fix: a joint-stock company would lend the crown the money at 8 percent interest, in exchange for a charter and the right to issue notes against the loan.

Charles Montagu steered the plan through Parliament as the Tonnage Act of 1694, and the money came fast: 1.2 million pounds from 1,268 subscribers inside twelve days. The royal charter followed on 27 July, creating the Governor and Company of the Bank of England as a lender to the state rather than a household name for savers.

The revolt began at an opera. On 25 August 1830 a Brussels audience watching Auber's La Muette de Portici rose at the duet Amour sacre de la patrie and poured into the streets shouting for revolt against Dutch rule. Within days crowds held the Parc de Bruxelles and the royal palace, and Dutch troops under Prince Frederik fought house to house for four days in September before withdrawing to their fortresses.

The great powers met in London that December and, with none of them willing to send troops to restore Dutch authority, recognised an independent Belgium. Leopold of Saxe-Coburg accepted the new throne and took his oath as king on 21 July 1831, a date still marked as Belgium's national day.

Stalin's blockade was aimed at a currency, not a city. When the Western powers introduced the Deutsche Mark into West Berlin in June 1948, Soviet forces cut every road, rail and canal link to the city to force its withdrawal. Rather than abandon the two million people left inside, Britain and the United States began flying in everything they needed.

The airlift ran for fifteen months, delivering over two million tons of coal, food and fuel across more than 200,000 flights, with a plane landing roughly every thirty seconds at its peak. One American pilot, Gail Halvorsen, began dropping small parcels of sweets to children below, a habit that grew into an organised effort called Operation Little Vittles.

Fourteen states sent delegates to Berlin between November 1884 and February 1885, including the United States and the Ottoman Empire alongside every major European power. Not one African ruler was invited; the Sultan of Zanzibar's request to attend was turned aside under pressure from anti-slavery campaigners who wanted the conference to look otherwise.

The resulting act confirmed King Leopold II's personal claim to the Congo through his International Congo Society and declared free trade along the Congo basin, but its lasting rule was that a claim to African territory needed actual occupation on the ground to be recognised. That single requirement set off a scramble among European powers to plant garrisons across the continent within a matter of months.

James Madison had argued against adding a bill of rights at all, calling the Constitution's structure protection enough. He changed course once it became clear that several states would only ratify with a promise of amendments attached, and he ended up drafting most of them himself in the First Congress.

Congress sent twelve articles to the states in 1789. Ten were ratified by 15 December 1791 and became the first ten amendments. One dealt with congressional pay and went nowhere for two centuries before finally becoming the Twenty-seventh Amendment in 1992; another, on the size of the House, has never been ratified at all.

The territory had no name of its own for most of the war, known simply as Upper Peru, a mountainous appendage of the Spanish empire fought over by armies from Buenos Aires and Lima alike. Antonio Jose de Sucre's campaign broke the last royalist resistance there in 1825, and delegates meeting at Chuquisaca that July had a real choice: join Peru, join Argentina, or stand alone.

They chose independence, and signed the declaration on 6 August 1825, naming the new republic after Simon Bolivar, who had led much of the wider South American struggle from the north. Bolivar was declared its first president but left within months to attend to Peru and Colombia, handing the country to Sucre, who governed it for the next several years.

Chief Justice Earl Warren wanted no dissent recorded, and on 17 May 1954 he got a unanimous 9 to 0 ruling. The Court held that separate schools for black and white children could never be equal, overturning the standard set almost sixty years earlier in Plessy v. Ferguson, which had allowed segregated facilities as long as they were nominally comparable.

The ruling itself set no deadline. A second decision the following year told districts to desegregate with all deliberate speed, a phrase vague enough that many Southern states spent years finding ways around it, from closing public schools outright to funding private academies that admitted only white students.

Aung San did not live to see the country he had negotiated free. On 19 July 1947 gunmen burst into a cabinet meeting in Rangoon's Secretariat Building and shot him along with eight of his colleagues, six months before the independence he had spent his life pursuing took effect on 4 January 1948.

Burma also made a choice few other former colonies made at that moment: it left the Commonwealth entirely rather than remain a dominion under the crown. Clement Attlee's government told parliament it regretted the decision, but the Burma Independence Act had already been drafted to allow for a country outside the King's dominions.

Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin spent thirteen days at Jimmy Carter's presidential retreat in Maryland, from 5 to 17 September 1978, in talks so tense that Carter reportedly kept the two leaders apart for much of it and shuttled between their cabins himself.

The result was two framework agreements, one sketching a broader Middle East settlement and one specifically for Egypt and Israel, signed at the White House. The bilateral framework led directly to the Egypt-Israel peace treaty the following March. Sadat and Begin shared the 1978 Nobel Peace Prize, though much of the Arab world condemned Egypt for negotiating alone.

The Carolingian line had not run out of heirs when Hugh Capet became king in 987. A cousin, Charles of Lower Lorraine, was still alive and had a claim, but he had made himself a vassal of the German emperor and the great lords of France would not accept him. Meeting at Senlis after King Louis V died childless, they chose Hugh instead, on the argument that a throne need not pass by blood alone.

Hugh was crowned twice within five weeks, at Noyon on 1 June and again at Paris on 3 July. That same year he had his own son Robert crowned as co-king, a precaution against exactly the kind of disputed succession that had just put him on the throne. The house he founded held the French crown, through cadet branches, for close to nine centuries.

For over two decades the Republic of China on Taiwan held China's seat at the United Nations, even as the Communist government in Beijing controlled the mainland. Albania led a group of seventeen member states pressing to correct what they called an anomaly rather than a genuine representation of China.

On 25 October 1971, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 2758, recognising the People's Republic of China as the sole legitimate representative of China and expelling the Taipei delegation. Beijing took both the Assembly seat and the permanent seat on the Security Council, a shift several NATO members and non-aligned states had voted to support.

Southern senators held the floor for 54 working days trying to talk the bill to death, Robert Byrd alone speaking for fourteen straight hours. Senator Richard Russell said openly that his side would resist to the end any measure bringing about what he called social equality. On 10 June 1964 the Senate voted 71 to 29 to cut off debate, the first time cloture had ever succeeded against a civil rights filibuster.

President Lyndon Johnson signed the bill on 2 July 1964, weeks after the vote that broke the filibuster. It reached that point only through a bipartisan rewrite led by Senators Mansfield, Humphrey, Dirksen and Kuchel, which pulled in enough Republican votes to survive the Southern bloc. The law banned segregation in public accommodations and schools, and discrimination in hiring.

Six separate British colonies, each with its own parliament, tariffs and railway gauge, spent the 1890s arguing over how much power a shared government should hold. Referendums settled the terms, and on 1 January 1901 the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution was proclaimed at Centennial Park in Sydney.

Edmund Barton was sworn in as interim prime minister that day, leading a ministry of nine before any election had been held. Federation kept the colonies as states inside a new bicameral parliament, with a governor-general representing the monarch, rather than dissolving them into one unified administration.

Henry Clay put five bills before the Senate in January 1850, and it was Stephen Douglas who broke them apart and steered each through Congress after Clay's health failed. California entered as a free state, ending Southern hopes of a slave-state belt to the Pacific, while Texas gave up its claim to New Mexico in return for the federal government taking on its debt.

New Mexico and Utah were organised on popular sovereignty, letting settlers vote on slavery rather than have Congress decide, and the slave trade, though not slaveholding itself, was banned in Washington. The compromise's sharpest edge was a strengthened Fugitive Slave Act, which denied accused runaways the right to testify and made helping them a federal crime.

No single document created it. The Concert of Europe grew out of the Congress of Vienna as an understanding among Austria, Britain, Prussia, Russia and later France that the great powers would settle disputes through conferences rather than let any one state upset the borders just redrawn. Its other purpose was blunter: putting down the liberal and nationalist uprisings that kept breaking out across the continent.

It never had fixed rules or a secretariat, just a habit of meeting when a crisis threatened to spiral, and historians argue over exactly when it stopped working. A first phase held roughly until the 1860s; a looser version limped on through rising nationalism and rigid alliance blocs until 1914, when a crisis in the Balkans finally proved too large for any congress to manage.

For fifty years popes and emperors had fought over a single question: who could appoint a bishop. Reformist popes, Gregory VII foremost among them, argued that a secular ruler had no authority to hand a churchman the ring and staff that marked his office. Emperors had done exactly that for generations, treating bishoprics as posts to reward loyal men.

Pope Callixtus II and Emperor Henry V settled it at Worms on 23 September 1122. Henry gave up the right to invest clergy with ring and crosier, leaving that to the Church, but kept a hand in elections and could still grant a bishop his temporal lands with a sceptre, a separate and later ceremony. The papal side put it plainly: the Church would have what belonged to Christ, and the emperor what belonged to him.

Delegates from across Europe gathered in Vienna from September 1814 to redraw the map after Napoleon's abdication, and Austria's foreign minister Metternich ran the show. France arrived defeated and largely excluded, yet Talleyrand talked his way into the inner circle anyway, playing the great powers off one another until France had a seat at the real decisions.

Then, in March 1815, Napoleon escaped Elba and marched on Paris. The delegates kept negotiating anyway, and the Final Act was signed on 9 June, nine days before Waterloo settled the matter for good. Between sessions there were enough balls and banquets that one Austrian diplomat is remembered for joking that the congress danced rather than worked.

When Muhammad arrived in Medina in 622, the city held Muslim migrants from Mecca, local converts, pagan Arab clans and several Jewish tribes, none bound to the others by blood or prior loyalty. The document he drew up made membership a matter of shared commitment rather than kinship, naming the signatories one community regardless of tribe.

Its terms let each group keep its own faith and law: for the Jews their religion, for the Muslims theirs, while requiring joint defence of the city and peaceful arbitration of disputes rather than the customary tribal retaliation. Muhammad sat as arbiter over the whole arrangement, a role no single clan chief in Medina had previously held.

The delegates who met at Pennsylvania's State House from late May 1787 were supposed to be revising the Articles of Confederation, not replacing them. Within days they had agreed to start over. Windows were nailed shut against the summer heat to keep the debates from leaking out, and no official transcript survives beyond a secretary's sparse minutes.

George Washington presided over roughly fifty-five delegates, though attendance on any given day was closer to thirty. Rhode Island sent nobody. James Madison's own notes, the fullest record of what was argued inside that sealed room, stayed unpublished until after his death in 1836. Thirty-nine of the fifty-five delegates present signed the finished Constitution on 17 September.

Emperor Constantine convened the bishops at Nicaea in 325 not out of theological conviction but to stop a quarrel splitting his newly unified church. The Alexandrian priest Arius had been teaching that Christ the Son was created by God the Father and therefore not equal to him or eternal, a position that had already caused riots in Egypt.

Roughly two to three hundred bishops attended, and the council sided against Arius, declaring the Son consubstantial with the Father in a creed that anathematised anyone who said there was a time before Christ existed. Arius was exiled, but his teaching outlived the verdict, resurfacing among Germanic kingdoms for centuries afterward.

The clay cylinder was buried as a foundation deposit under a temple wall in Babylon and stayed there until Hormuzd Rassam dug it up for the British Museum in 1879. Its cuneiform text is a building inscription in a familiar Mesopotamian form: it damns the deposed king Nabonidus, credits the god Marduk with choosing Cyrus, and describes his entry into the city and his restoration of temples and displaced peoples.

Calling it the first charter of human rights is a twentieth century reading. The Shah's government promoted that phrase in 1971, and a copy still sits at the United Nations, but most specialists treat it as a conventional royal inscription following a much older genre, not a legal or political declaration. What is not disputed is Cyrus's own claim to have returned exiled peoples and their gods to their homes.

Germany had defaulted on reparations payments, and in 1923 France and Belgium answered by occupying the Ruhr, Germany's industrial heartland, to seize goods directly. The crisis that followed helped drive German hyperinflation to its worst. An American committee chaired by the banker Charles G. Dawes was called in to break the deadlock rather than punish it further.

The plan Dawes produced, adopted in 1924, lowered Germany's annual payments and staggered them upward over five years, while a foreign loan, much of it raised on Wall Street, recapitalised the German central bank. It eased the crisis without settling the underlying sum owed, and by 1929 a second scheme, the Young Plan, replaced it.

The capital's location was settled over dinner, more or less. Alexander Hamilton wanted northern votes for his plan to have the federal government assume state war debts; Thomas Jefferson and James Madison wanted the capital on the Potomac for southern states. The trade became the Residence Act, signed in July 1790, with Philadelphia serving as a ten-year stopgap while the new city was built.

George Washington picked the exact site the following year, a diamond of land straddling the river and taking in Georgetown and Alexandria. Pierre Charles L'Enfant laid out its broad avenues, though he was fired within a year over disputes with the commissioners overseeing the project. The government did not actually move in until 1800.

On New Year's Day 1942, the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union and China signed a pledge in Washington to fight the Axis with their full military and economic strength and not to seek a separate peace. Twenty-two further governments added their names the next day, and the tally reached forty-seven by the time the war ended.

Roosevelt had coined the phrase United Nations for the wartime coalition, and this declaration is where the name first carried legal weight rather than serving as a slogan. The commitments it wrote down against separate peace and pooled resources became the basis on which the permanent organisation was built three years later in San Francisco.

Seventeen African territories became independent states in 1960, more than in any other single year before or since. Most had been French possessions, including Chad, Gabon, Ivory Coast and the Republic of the Congo, whose independence days clustered through July and August. Nigeria, by far the most populous of the new states, followed on 1 October.

The pace was set less by any single agreement than by exhaustion on the colonial side and organised pressure on the other: France had already granted its territories self-government in 1958 and found full independence hard to refuse once the first few asked. The wave left several new borders, drawn decades earlier by colonial administrators, essentially unchanged.

Sparta had led the Greek war effort at Plataea and Mycale, then lost interest in chasing the Persians further. Athens took over, and in 478 BCE delegates from the Aegean city-states met on the sacred island of Delos to found a new alliance, pooling ships and money to keep fighting Persia and to divide whatever spoils came of it. The League's treasury sat on Delos itself, watched over by Athenian officials.

Membership was not really optional once a city had joined: those that tried to leave were besieged back into line. In 454 BCE the treasury moved to Athens, officially for safekeeping, though Pericles then spent some of it on Athenian building projects, the Parthenon among them. By the middle of the century a defensive alliance had become, in practice, an Athenian empire that collected tribute from its allies.

Diocletian did not carve the empire into two halves in a single stroke. He raised Maximian to co-ruler in 286, then in 293 added two junior emperors, Galerius and Constantius, each titled Caesar under a senior Augustus. Four courts, four armies, one frontier problem each: the empire had grown too large for one man to campaign and administer at once.

The system was built to survive its own founders' retirement. In 305 Diocletian and Maximian stepped down together, letting their Caesars rise smoothly to Augustus. It held for one cycle. When Constantius died in 306, his troops proclaimed his son Constantine emperor on the spot, ignoring the succession plan, and the tetrarchy unravelled into rival claimants within a generation.

The British North America Act, passed at Westminster, joined the Province of Canada, split into Ontario and Quebec, with Nova Scotia and New Brunswick on 1 July 1867. Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland stayed out at the time, unconvinced the arrangement suited them, and would join decades later on separate terms.

John A. Macdonald, who had lobbied hard for confederation at conferences in Charlottetown and Quebec City, became the new dominion's first prime minister after elections that August and September. Westminster still controlled foreign policy and constitutional amendment, so the country was not yet independent, a status worked out gradually over the following century.

The Act of Abjuration, agreed in July 1581, released the Dutch provinces from their oath to Philip II on the grounds that a king who oppressed his subjects and violated their rights had forfeited his claim to rule them. Officials were told to strike his name and seal from coins and legal documents and swear new oaths to their own provincial States instead.

It was not, at first, a bid to rule themselves. The provinces offered the crown to Francis, Duke of Anjou, and later courted Elizabeth I of England, who sent troops but declined the throne. Only after both efforts failed, and after William the Silent's assassination in 1584, did the States General settle into governing as a republic rather than hunting for a new king.

Elizabeth I granted the charter on the last day of 1600, to a group of London merchants under the cumbersome title of the Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies. It gave them a fifteen-year monopoly on English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope, backed by the threat of seizing the ships of anyone who tried to compete with them.

What began as a trading venture grew into something closer to a government. By the mid-1700s it kept its own private army, and after the Battle of Plassey in 1757 it started ruling Indian territory directly rather than just trading in it. The Crown did not take that power back until 1858, and the company itself was not dissolved until 1874.

Cassius Dio, writing not long after, thought he knew the real motive: more taxpayers. Only citizens owed certain Roman taxes, so an emperor who made every free man in the empire a citizen also made every one of them liable for revenue that provincials had previously escaped. Caracalla issued the edict in 212 CE, and it applied to free women across the empire as well.

A narrower class, the dediticii, mostly people who had surrendered under treaty or freed slaves branded with a criminal record, were left out. Historians also point to a simpler pressure behind the timing: only citizens could serve in the legions proper, so widening citizenship widened the pool the army could recruit from. Roman law itself had to be rewritten piecemeal afterward to fit provincial custom into rules built for citizens alone.

The document agreed at Milan in February 313 did not put Christianity in charge of anything. Constantine and his co-emperor Licinius extended toleration to every religion, ordering confiscated Christian property returned and compensation paid, but stopping well short of an official state faith. That step waited until 380, under Theodosius I, nearly seventy years later.

It was also never quite an edict issued at Milan. Historians now read it as a letter Licinius sent to provincial governors later that year from Nicomedia, after defeating a rival in the east, repeating terms the two emperors had settled on in person. The meeting behind it was real; the paperwork travelled separately.

Henry IV had converted to Catholicism himself to take the throne, but the edict he signed at Nantes in April 1598 let his former co-religionists worship without being harassed for it. Huguenots could hold public office, keep their own courts and universities, and garrison a number of fortified towns at the crown's expense, though Catholicism stayed the official religion and Protestants still paid its tithes.

It held for nearly ninety years. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685, ordering ministers out of France within two weeks and banning most other Protestants from leaving at all. Roughly 400,000 fled regardless, into England, Prussia and the Dutch Republic, taking skills and capital with them that France did not recover for a long time.

Seven states signed the Stockholm Convention on 4 January 1960 and formed the association that May: Austria, Denmark, Norway, Portugal, Sweden, Switzerland and the United Kingdom, nicknamed the Outer Seven against the EEC's inner six. Britain led the push after deciding it would not accept the deeper political union the EEC's founders wanted.

EFTA's members kept their own tariffs against the rest of the world and simply removed them among themselves, unlike the EEC's shared external wall. The looser design suited Britain, Denmark and Norway only for a while: all three later applied to join the EEC instead, and Britain's 1973 departure from EFTA reshaped an organisation that had been built partly around it.

Egypt agreed to something no other Arab state had accepted: recognising Israel outright. The treaty, signed at the White House on 26 March 1979, followed the Camp David framework and set out Israel's staged withdrawal from the Sinai Peninsula, which it had occupied since the 1967 war, in exchange for a demilitarised buffer and normal diplomatic relations.

The peace cost Egypt its place in the Arab League, which suspended the country from 1979 until 1989 over what other members called a unilateral betrayal of the Palestinian cause. Anwar Sadat, who had staked his presidency on the treaty, was assassinated by Islamist militants in October 1981.

Elizabeth was in Kenya, not London, when she became queen. She and Philip had spent the previous night watching wildlife from a treehouse hotel called Treetops before returning to their lodge on the morning of 6 February 1952, where Philip told her that her father, George VI, had died in his sleep at Sandringham.

She chose to keep her own name rather than adopt a new regnal title, becoming Elizabeth II, and the couple cut short a planned tour of Australia and New Zealand to fly home. There was no coronation for another sixteen months; it took that long to prepare Westminster Abbey and rehearse a ceremony that had not been performed since 1937.

Lincoln issued a preliminary warning in September 1862 and the proclamation itself took effect on 1 January 1863. It applied only to the ten states still in rebellion, naming them individually, and explicitly excluded the loyal border states of Missouri, Kentucky, Maryland and Delaware along with several Union-held counties and parishes in the South.

Lincoln had no authority to free enslaved people anywhere the federal government did not control, so the order reached them only as Union troops advanced; immediate freedom in areas already occupied touched perhaps 25,000 to 75,000 people out of more than three million covered on paper. Roughly 300,000 more, in the exempted areas, gained nothing from it at all.

Simon de Montfort had already beaten King Henry III in battle once, at Lewes in 1264, and ruled through a council in the king's name. For his 1265 parliament he went further than any English summons before it, writing to the sheriffs to summon barons and bishops alongside two elected representatives from each county and from a chosen list of towns, ordinary men with no title at all.

It did not save him. Prince Edward escaped custody that May and gathered marcher lords and defectors, among them the powerful Gilbert de Clare. At Evesham on 4 August 1265, a little over a year after the parliament, Edward's men marched under Montfort's own captured banners, and Montfort realised who they were only when it was too late.

Britain and France had nearly gone to war over African territory as recently as 1898. The 1904 agreement traded recognition: France accepted British control of Egypt, Britain accepted French influence in Morocco, and a separate clause guaranteed free passage through the Suez Canal.

Smaller disputes came with it. France gave up fishing rights off Newfoundland's coast, Britain handed over territory in West Africa, and the two sides split spheres of influence in Siam. The document was not a military alliance, and said so, but it opened the door to joint staff talks between the two armies in the years that followed.

Robert Schuman put the proposal in blunt terms on 9 May 1950: pool French and German coal and steel production under one authority, and war between the two countries would become unthinkable, and in material terms impossible. Coal and steel were the raw materials of armies as much as factories, which was exactly why he chose them.

France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg signed the treaty establishing the Community the following year, placing their heavy industry under a supranational High Authority rather than national ministries. It was a modest arrangement in scope but a new kind of institution, one that member states answered to rather than merely negotiated with.

Eleven ships left Portsmouth in May 1787 carrying roughly 1,400 people, most of them convicts, on a voyage of eight months to the far side of the world. They reached Botany Bay in January 1788, the site James Cook had recommended eighteen years earlier, only for Governor Arthur Phillip to find it open to the sea, short of fresh water and poorly soiled.

Phillip sailed a few kilometres north and found a deep, sheltered harbour he judged one of the finest anywhere. The fleet moved in and raised the flag at Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788, the date Australia now marks as a national holiday, though for the Eora people already living there it began something very different: dispossession followed within years.

Kadesh itself had settled nothing. Ramesses II and the Hittite king Muwatalli II fought to a bloody standstill around 1274 BCE, and each side went home claiming victory. It took sixteen more years, a change of Hittite king to Hattusili III, and shared fear of a rising Assyria before the two empires finally put the argument on paper.

The tablet found at Hattusa and the hieroglyphic copy in Egypt bind both kings to non-aggression, mutual defence against a third party, and the extradition of refugees and criminals. Each version names the other side's gods as witnesses. Ramesses also married a Hittite princess, and the peace held for roughly eighty years, until the Hittite state collapsed.

London, not New York, hosted the United Nations' first working session. Delegates from 51 founding nations gathered at Methodist Central Hall on 10 January 1946, a building better known for church conferences than international diplomacy, because no permanent headquarters yet existed anywhere.

The organisation spent its early years without a fixed home, meeting later in a former World's Fair pavilion in Flushing Meadows before Manhattan construction finished in 1951. That itinerant period included one of the Assembly's most consequential early votes, the November 1947 decision to partition Palestine, taken not in London but at the temporary Flushing site.

Theodor Herzl had wanted to hold the congress in Munich, but Jewish community leaders there, uneasy about a political movement built around a homeland in Palestine, pushed him out. He moved it to Basel instead, where 208 delegates from seventeen countries gathered in the Stadtcasino concert hall from 29 to 31 August 1897.

More than half the delegates came from Eastern Europe, and seventeen women attended, though without a vote. The congress adopted the Basel Program, stating that Zionism sought a home for the Jewish people in Palestine secured under public law, and founded the Zionist Organization with Herzl as its president to pursue it.

Lafayette drafted an early version with Thomas Jefferson, then the American minister in Paris, looking over his shoulder, before the National Constituent Assembly rewrote it into seventeen short articles and adopted it on 26 August 1789. It swept away noble exemptions from taxation and declared that law applies equally to everyone, a direct answer to a monarchy built on inherited privilege.

The articles said little about who counted as a citizen in practice. Olympe de Gouges would answer with her own Declaration of the Rights of Woman three years later, and slavery in France's colonies was not abolished until 1794, then restored under Napoleon. The 1789 text itself survives largely unchanged, now written into the preamble of the French constitution.

The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade was meant as a stopgap. Twenty-three nations signed it in Geneva on 30 October 1947 while a much larger body, the proposed International Trade Organization, was still being negotiated among more than fifty countries. When the United States withdrew from that larger project, the stopgap became the only working framework for world trade.

GATT ran on that improvised basis for nearly half a century, through repeated rounds of tariff cuts, before it was finally given a permanent institution. On 1 January 1995 the World Trade Organization took over its functions, and the seventy six governments that had belonged to GATT became its founding members.

Delegates from a dozen European states met in Geneva in August 1864 and signed an agreement built directly on Henry Dunant's proposals from the previous year. It bound signatory armies to spare field hospitals and ambulances from attack and to treat wounded soldiers from any side without distinction once they were disabled from fighting.

Medical staff and the civilians helping them were granted protection as non-combatants, and the treaty gave the red cross on a white ground legal standing as the sign marking anyone and anything covered by these rules. It was the first multilateral treaty of its kind, and every later Geneva Convention was built as an addition to it.

The four conventions adopted in 1949 were written by people who had just read the Nuremberg and Tokyo trial records. Earlier Geneva agreements had covered wounded soldiers and prisoners of war; this revision added a fourth convention protecting civilians, the population that had suffered the war's occupations, sieges and camps with the least legal protection of all.

Together the four texts set out rules for the wounded and sick in the field, the wounded and shipwrecked at sea, the treatment of prisoners of war, and civilians under occupation. Nearly every state in the world has since ratified them, in whole or with reservations, giving them a reach that few other treaties from the period can match.

Emperor Charles IV issued the Golden Bull at imperial diets in Nuremberg and Metz in 1356, and it did something no earlier decree had managed: it fixed exactly who could choose the next King of the Romans and how. Seven electors got the vote, the archbishops of Mainz, Cologne and Trier, and the secular rulers of Bohemia, the Rhineland Palatinate, Saxony-Wittenberg and Brandenburg.

Four votes out of seven were enough to elect an emperor, so no minority of three could block a decision forever. The electoral territories themselves were made indivisible, closing off the kind of family partition that had fragmented other German titles. The Bull said nothing about needing papal approval for any of it, a silence that quietly ended Rome's old claim to confirm the choice.

The dynasty took its name from an obscure ruler simply called Gupta, whose kingdom around 240 was modest. Its real rise came under his grandson Chandragupta I, who took the throne around 320 after marrying Kumaradevi, a princess of the Licchavi clan. That marriage brought territory and prestige enough for him to claim the grand title Maharajadhiraja, king of kings.

What followed is remembered less for conquest than for output. Under Chandragupta's successors, the mathematician Aryabhata worked out a value for pi and described the earth's rotation, while Kalidasa wrote Sanskrit poetry still read today. None of it required a battle: the Gupta court funded scholars and let them work.

Anthony Ashley-Cooper, Earl of Shaftesbury, pushed the bill through a Parliament trying to keep the Catholic James, Duke of York, from the throne, and feared what an unrestrained monarch might do to critics in the meantime. The mechanism it strengthened was old: a prisoner could demand a writ ordering a jailer to bring them before a judge and justify the detention.

What was new was the enforcement. The Act barred jailers from shipping a prisoner abroad or shuffling them between prisons to dodge that writ, and it fined any jailer who tried, with the money going to the prisoner. It covered most criminal detentions, though not treason or felony charges, and left the writ itself as the tool later invoked against arbitrary confinement far beyond England.

Tsar Nicholas II called the conference, and it opened on 18 May 1899, his own birthday, at the House in the Wood near The Hague. Delegates from 26 states banned poison, the killing of surrendered soldiers, looting and collective punishment, and required humane treatment of prisoners.

A separate declaration outlawed dropping projectiles from balloons for five years and banned soft-nosed bullets that flattened on impact, a rule aimed at ammunition nicknamed after the Dum Dum arsenal in India. The conference also created the Permanent Court of Arbitration, the first standing body for settling disputes between states without war.

The Qin state's own capital fell within four years of the emperor's death, and out of the scramble that followed came two rival commanders, Liu Bang and Xiang Yu. Liu Bang, a commoner who had once worked as a minor local official, took the title King of Han in 206 BCE and then finished off Xiang Yu at Gaixia in 202 BCE, becoming Emperor Gaozu of a reunified China.

The dynasty he founded gave China its ethnonym, the Han people, and lasted on and off for four centuries. Under his successors it pushed the Silk Road west, standardised coinage, and produced papermaking and early seismometers. Emperor Wu later made Confucian learning the basis of the civil service, a system for selecting officials that outlasted the dynasty itself by well over a thousand years.

The Hanseatic League never had a founding ceremony, and no single document created it. What happened in 1241 was narrower: Lubeck, sitting on both the Baltic and North Sea trade routes, struck an alliance with Hamburg to protect the roads between them from robbery and tolls. The word Hanse itself would not appear in a document for another twenty six years.

Out of that arrangement grew a network that eventually took in close to two hundred towns across what are now eight countries. Hanseatic ships carried furs, wax, timber and grain west and cloth east, and Bergen's stockfish moved south in exchange for grain. By the time of the Treaty of Stralsund in 1370 the League could fight and win a war against the King of Denmark.

Thirty-five states, nearly every country in Europe alongside the United States and Canada, signed the Helsinki Final Act between 30 July and 1 August 1975. It was not a treaty and carried no enforcement mechanism, only a political commitment covering security, economic cooperation and, in its most contested section, human rights.

Soviet negotiators treated the human rights clauses as a formality that cost them little for Western recognition of Cold War borders. Dissidents inside the Eastern bloc read them differently, and used the accords to found monitoring groups, among them Helsinki Watch, which later grew into Human Rights Watch.

Charlemagne had already been crowned emperor once, in 800, but that title lapsed after his line's power collapsed. When Pope John XII placed a crown on Otto I in 962, he was reviving a defunct office rather than inventing one, giving the German kings a claim to stand as Charlemagne's successors in the west.

Otto had already spent over a decade consolidating power in Germany and northern Italy before the coronation, defeating rival dukes and a Magyar invasion at the Lechfeld. The empire that took shape around his crown had no fixed capital and no single language, a loose federation of princes under an emperor that would outlast most of its neighbours by centuries.

The organisation did not emerge from a labour congress but from a peace treaty. Its founding report was folded into Part XIII of the Treaty of Versailles, adopted at the Paris peace conference on 11 April 1919, on the argument that lasting peace required decent conditions for workers rather than the resentment that had helped produce the war.

Its structure was unusual for the time: governments, employers and workers each sent delegates, though governments held twice the votes of the other two groups combined. The first International Labour Conference met in Washington in October 1919 and adopted six conventions at once, setting limits on working hours and banning most child labour.

By 1493 the empire ruled from Cusco stretched north into what is now Ecuador and Colombia and south along the Andes, held together not by a single army garrisoning it but by the Qhapaq Nan, a road network reaching almost every province it controlled.

Population estimates run from six to fourteen million, a range so wide partly because the Incas kept their records on knotted cords called quipu, most of which the Spanish later destroyed. Households owed labour rather than goods under the mit'a system, which built the roads, bridges and storehouses that made the empire's size workable at all.

B.R. Ambedkar chaired the seven member committee that spent nearly three years drafting the document, sitting through eleven sessions of the Constituent Assembly before it was finished. What they produced remains the longest written constitution of any country, running to 395 articles and eight schedules by the time it took effect on 26 January 1950.

The date was chosen deliberately: 26 January had already been marked twenty years earlier as Purna Swaraj day, when the Indian National Congress first declared full independence as a goal rather than a distant hope. Rajendra Prasad took office as the republic's first president on the same day the document came into force.

A lawyer named Cyril Radcliffe, who had never set foot in India before, was given five weeks in the summer of 1947 to draw the border splitting Punjab and Bengal between two new countries. He worked from out of date maps and census returns, and the line he produced was published only after independence had already taken effect on 14 and 15 August.

Estimates of the dead from the migrations that followed range from roughly 200,000 to two million, a gap that reflects how little the movement of people across the new border was ever formally counted. Between twelve and twenty million people crossed it in one direction or the other, on foot, by cart, and by train.

Andrew Jackson signed the act on 28 May 1830, authorising the government to trade land west of the Mississippi for tribal territory in the southeast. It did not name a single tribe, but its target was the land held by the Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw and Seminole nations, whose removal Jackson framed as an exchange rather than an expulsion.

The Cherokee fought removal in the courts and won a Supreme Court ruling in their favour, which Jackson's administration simply ignored. Federal troops marched roughly 16,000 Cherokee west in the winter of 1838 and 1839 along what became known as the Trail of Tears; thousands died of cold, disease and starvation on the way, one of at least eighteen tribes displaced under the act.

Jawaharlal Nehru and Mohammad Ayub Khan signed the treaty in Karachi on 19 September 1960, alongside a World Bank official whose institution had spent nearly a decade brokering the deal. Rather than sharing each river, the treaty split the Indus system in two: India got the three eastern tributaries, the Ravi, Beas and Sutlej, while Pakistan got the larger western ones, the Indus, Chenab and Jhelum.

The split was lopsided by volume, roughly eighty percent of the combined flow going to Pakistan, but it gave each side clear control rather than a shared tap either could dispute. The treaty survived wars between the two countries in 1965, 1971 and 1999 without either side suspending it, a record that outlasted most of what else the two nations agreed that decade.

The Anglo-Irish Treaty, signed in December 1921, gave the new state dominion status equal to Canada's rather than full separation, and the Free State itself came into being on 6 December 1922. Members of its parliament had to swear an oath naming both the state and the king, a form of words republicans found impossible to accept and refused to take.

Northern Ireland, six of Ireland's thirty two counties, used a right written into the treaty to opt straight back out the following day, leaving the Free State with the remaining twenty six. A boundary commission was meant to redraw the border afterward, though its work never produced the changes either side expected.

David Ben-Gurion read the proclamation at the Tel Aviv Museum on the afternoon of 14 May 1948, and it took him sixteen minutes. The building had no name yet fit for the occasion; it is now called Independence Hall. Within hours the United States had extended recognition, and the Soviet Union followed three days later with formal diplomatic recognition.

Troops from Egypt, Transjordan, Iraq and Syria crossed into the territory the next morning, opening a war that ran into 1949. By its end Israel held about half again the land the United Nations partition plan had allotted it, and more than 700,000 Palestinian Arabs had fled or been expelled from the areas that became Israeli territory.

The Virginia Company's settlers built James Fort on a swampy peninsula in May 1607, choosing the site for its defensible position rather than its water or soil. Both proved bad choices: a severe drought had already begun, and within the first year roughly two thirds of the original settlers were dead before a resupply fleet reached them in 1608.

The worst came later. Through the winter of 1609 to 1610, remembered as the Starving Time, colonists ate dogs, horses and boiled shoe leather, and evidence uncovered by archaeologists shows some resorted to eating the dead. Of the 214 people counted in one supply mission, only 60 survived until a relief fleet under Thomas West arrived in June 1610 and kept the colony from being abandoned.

Frank Kellogg, the American secretary of state, and Aristide Briand, France's foreign minister, put their names to an agreement signed in Paris on 27 August 1928, in which the signing states renounced war as a tool of policy. Fifteen nations signed that day, and within a decade the number of adherents had climbed past sixty, drawing in most of the world's governments.

The pact carried no mechanism to enforce itself: it named no penalty beyond withdrawing the treaty's own benefits from a violator, and the United States Senate made clear that ratification bound the country to nothing further. States kept fighting without formally declaring war, a habit the pact did nothing to stop, though its wording later helped shape the postwar legal case against wars of aggression.

Ibn Saud had spent three decades taking Arabia region by region, starting with his 1902 recapture of Riyadh, then Nejd by 1921 and the Hejaz, with Mecca, by 1925. Rather than merge them at once, he ruled Nejd and the Hejaz as separate kingdoms under his own crown for several years, an arrangement that kept older loyalties intact while power stayed with him alone.

On 23 September 1932 he combined the two into a single state, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, with himself as king. The date is still marked as the country's national day. The unification gave the new kingdom control of the Hejaz's pilgrimage cities, a source of both prestige and revenue that oil would not rival for another decade.

Puyi was five years old and had no idea what was happening. On 12 February 1912 his regent, the Empress Dowager Longyu, signed the abdication edict on his behalf, a deal brokered by general Yuan Shikai between the collapsing court and the republicans of the Xinhai Revolution.

The new republic let Puyi keep his title and stay inside the Forbidden City with a household and an annual subsidy, and for some time nobody told him his reign had actually ended. He believed himself emperor still, a fiction the palace maintained until his eventual eviction in 1924, twelve years after the edict he never understood he had signed away.

Spain's grip on its American colonies had been slipping for a decade before 1821, ever since Napoleon's invasion of Spain itself left the crown too weak to govern from across the ocean. In Mexico, a former royalist officer named Agustin de Iturbide switched sides, joined forces with insurgents under the Army of the Three Guarantees, and marched into Mexico City that September without a final battle.

Elsewhere the fighting had been much harder won. Simon Bolivar and Jose de San Martin had spent years campaigning across the Andes and the northern coast, and by the early 1820s most of Spanish South America had followed Mexico out of the empire. Spain kept Cuba and Puerto Rico for another seven decades, but its mainland American empire was effectively gone within a few years of Mexico's break.

The alliance signed at Cambrai in December 1508 called itself a crusade against the Ottomans. Its real purpose sat in secret clauses: France, the Holy Roman Empire, Aragon and the Papal States had agreed to carve up Venice's mainland territory between them, alarmed by how far the republic's holdings had spread across northern Italy.

It did not survive its own success. Once Venice had been badly beaten in the field, Pope Julius II grew more worried about French power in Italy than about Venice, and switched sides in 1510. Aragon followed him into a new Holy League against France, and by 1512 the emperor made his own truce with Venice, leaving the coalition that had formed against it in ruins.

Philip II did not need to persuade the Greek cities so much as defeat them first. After crushing Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BCE, he called the survivors to Corinth and offered terms that looked generous on paper: each city kept its own constitution, free navigation, and a promise of no interference in internal affairs, all guaranteed by a common oath.

The guarantee came with Macedonian garrisons at Corinth, Thebes, Ambracia and Pydna, which made refusal difficult. The League's council named Philip supreme commander for a planned invasion of Persia, a campaign his assassination in 336 BCE prevented him from leading. His son Alexander inherited both the title and the war.

Woodrow Wilson had pushed hardest for it at the Paris peace talks, and its covenant was largely drafted by two other men, Britain's Lord Robert Cecil and South Africa's Jan Smuts. The League came into being on 10 January 1920 with an Assembly, a Council and a permanent secretariat based in Geneva.

Wilson won the Nobel Peace Prize for the idea, then watched his own Senate refuse it. Republican opponents led by Henry Cabot Lodge kept the treaty short of the two thirds majority it needed on 19 March 1920, and the United States never joined the organisation its own president had designed.

John Adams signed the legislation on 24 April 1800, setting aside five thousand dollars for books a moving government would need once it left Philadelphia for the new capital. The whole collection fit into a room in the Capitol: 740 volumes and three maps, ordered from London for members of Congress to consult.

It did not survive the decade intact. British troops burned the Capitol in August 1814 and destroyed most of what had been bought, leaving only a single account book that an officer took as a souvenir and that was not returned to the United States until 1940. Thomas Jefferson sold Congress his own library, nearly 6,500 books, to rebuild the collection the following year.

Seven governments negotiated at Locarno in October 1925: Germany, France, Belgium, Britain, Italy, Poland and Czechoslovakia. The core deal bound Germany, France and Belgium to accept their shared borders as fixed by Versailles, with Britain and Italy standing as guarantors. Germany would not extend the same acceptance eastward, leaving its frontiers with Poland and Czechoslovakia open to future revision.

The arrangement also committed Germany to keep the Rhineland demilitarised. It held for barely a decade: on 7 March 1936 German troops marched back into the zone, and the other signatories issued verbal protest but took no military response. The treaties stayed nominally in force, but the Rhineland's remilitarisation had already made them dead letter.

Robert Livingston and James Monroe went to Paris in 1803 with instructions to buy New Orleans, nothing more. French treasury minister Barbe-Marbois instead offered the entire territory west of the Mississippi. Napoleon had lost interest in a New World empire after an army sent to crush a slave uprising in Haiti was decimated by fighting and disease.

The Americans settled on fifteen million dollars for roughly 828,000 square miles, under three cents an acre, doubling the size of the country without a shot fired. The deal left the new republic with a stake in a struggle it refused to acknowledge: when Haiti declared independence the following year, the United States would not recognise it and backed a trade embargo instead.

Nobody signed Magna Carta. King John pressed his seal into wax at Runnymede on 15 June 1215, since a medieval king authenticated a document that way, not with a signature. A council of twenty five barons was set up to make sure he kept to it. He did not, and within ten weeks Pope Innocent III had annulled the charter, tipping England into the First Barons' War.

The document that mattered was not the one at Runnymede. It was reissued in 1216 stripped of its sharpest clauses, again in 1217 as part of a peace settlement, and again in 1225 by Henry III in exchange for a new tax grant. Edward I confirmed it as statute law in 1297, and it was that later, revised text, not John's, that entered English law.

Japan's Kwantung Army had seized Manchuria by force through 1931, and on 1 March 1932 it proclaimed the territory an independent state, Manchukuo, with its capital at Changchun, renamed Xinjing. To give the new state a face other than a Japanese general's, it installed Puyi, the last emperor of the Qing dynasty, first as regent and later, in 1934, as emperor under the name Kangde.

Puyi signed decrees and held ceremony, but the Kwantung Army's commander doubled as Japan's ambassador and could veto him outright, while Japanese vice-ministers embedded in every department made the actual decisions. Manchukuo issued its own currency and stamps and joined no meaningful international body; only a handful of states, chiefly Japan's allies, ever recognised it.

George Marshall chose a Harvard commencement, not a press conference, to announce American aid for Europe on 5 June 1947. He spoke for under twenty minutes and named no figures, leaving the detail to Congress, which eventually voted through roughly twelve billion dollars over four years once Truman signed the programme into law the following spring.

Stalin briefly weighed joining before Molotov walked out of the Paris talks that would have committed the Soviet Union to open its books to American oversight. Moscow then barred the Eastern Bloc from accepting any aid and answered with its own Molotov Plan, calling Marshall's programme a scheme for the economic enslavement of Europe.

Little about Chandragupta's rise is independently confirmed. Buddhist, Jain and Hindu sources agree that he overthrew the Nanda dynasty around 322 BCE with the help of an advisor, Chanakya, but historians treat much of the detail as legend grown up around a real conquest rather than a reliable record.

What is clearer is the scale of what followed: Chandragupta pushed Greek garrisons left behind by Alexander out of the Punjab, then fought his way toward the Nanda capital at Pataliputra, taking territory and installing garrisons as he advanced. The empire he founded eventually stretched from Afghanistan into the Deccan, the first to unify most of the Indian subcontinent under one ruler.

The Mayflower had been chartered for Virginia, but storms pushed it to Cape Cod instead, well outside the territory its passengers had permission to settle. Some of the non-Puritan passengers on board, travelling for their own reasons rather than religious ones, argued that landing outside the agreed patent released them from any obligation to obey Pilgrim leadership.

To head off that argument, 41 of the men on board signed a short compact on 21 November 1620, agreeing to form a body politic and submit to whatever just laws it later passed for the colony's good. It pledged loyalty to James I in the same breath, and gave Plymouth a working government before a single building had been raised ashore.

Behind the restoration lay the domains of Satsuma and Choshu, rivals turned allies who had watched foreign warships force open Japanese ports and decided the shogunate could not be trusted to answer them. On 3 January 1868 their forces backed a declaration that political power was returned to the Imperial House, ending the Tokugawa shogunate that had ruled Japan since 1603.

Emperor Meiji, still a teenager, became the nominal centre of a government run largely by the domain leaders who had put him there. Within a few years the samurai class was dissolved, the old domains replaced with prefectures, and a programme of rapid industrialisation and Western-style institutions was under way.

Zhu Yuanzhang began as a penniless peasant and a Buddhist monk before joining the Red Turban rebels in 1352, during a wave of uprisings against Mongol Yuan rule brought on by heavy taxation and Yellow River flooding that the Yuan government had left unmanaged. He took Nanjing in 1356 and spent the next years crushing rival rebel leaders, most decisively Chen Youliang at the Battle of Lake Poyang in 1363.

With his rivals gone he marched north in 1368, and the last Yuan emperor fled the capital rather than fight. Zhu declared the Ming dynasty and took the era name Hongwu, meaning vastly martial. His rise ended roughly a century of Mongol rule over China and restored a Han Chinese imperial house for the first time since the Song.

Missouri's request to join the Union in 1819 threatened to tip the Senate's careful balance between slave and free states. The deadlock broke only when Illinois senator Jesse Thomas added a separate provision: Missouri would enter as a slave state, Maine would be carved off from Massachusetts and enter free, and the balance would hold at twelve states each.

Thomas's clause did the lasting work. It banned slavery from the rest of the Louisiana Purchase territory north of the 36 degree 30 minute line, leaving Missouri itself as the one exception north of that mark. The line held for over three decades before the Kansas-Nebraska Act unraveled it in 1854, and the Supreme Court struck it down as unconstitutional in the Dred Scott case of 1857.

When Genghis Khan died in 1227 his empire was already twice the size of the Roman Empire at its height. His successors kept expanding it for another two generations. Kublai Khan finished the conquest of Song China in 1279, folding the richest and most populous country on earth into a realm that already ran from Siberia to the edge of Eastern Europe.

By 1294 the Mongol domain covered roughly 23.5 million square kilometres, still the largest contiguous land empire ever assembled under one family. It was never one government for long: within decades of Kublai's death it had split into rival khanates that fought each other as readily as they had once fought outsiders.

President James Monroe delivered the line in his annual message to Congress on 2 December 1823, but the wording was chiefly the work of his secretary of state, John Quincy Adams. It declared the Americas closed to further European colonisation and warned that any attempt to extend a European monarchy's system into the hemisphere would be treated as a threat to the United States itself.

Adams had pushed for a unilateral statement rather than a joint declaration with Britain, wanting the United States to speak for itself even though its navy could not yet have enforced the warning against a determined European power. The doctrine had little practical effect for decades, and it was later presidents, not Monroe, who invoked it to justify direct intervention across Latin America.

A white mob rampaged through Springfield, Illinois in 1908, burning Black-owned homes and lynching two men within walking distance of Abraham Lincoln's tomb. The outrage pushed journalist William English Walling, social worker Mary White Ovington and Henry Moskowitz to call a meeting in New York that January.

Sixty prominent Americans signed the founding call, among them W. E. B. Du Bois, Ida B. Wells and Mary Church Terrell. The group formed on 12 February 1909, timed to the centenary of Lincoln's birth. Boston attorney Moorfield Storey, who was white, became its first president, while Du Bois ran publicity and edited its magazine.

Twelve countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington on 4 April 1949, building on an earlier and smaller pact among Belgium, France, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Britain. The new treaty pulled in the United States and Canada alongside Portugal, Italy, Norway, Denmark and Iceland, countries with little in common beyond a shared unease about Soviet intentions in Europe.

Its core clause, Article 5, commits every member to treat an attack on one as an attack on all. The wording was deliberately vague about what a response must involve, a compromise that let the United States join a peacetime European alliance for the first time in its history without binding Congress to any automatic declaration of war.

Franklin Roosevelt took office on 4 March 1933 with roughly a quarter of the workforce unemployed and the banking system seizing up under runs. Within days his Emergency Banking Act closed every bank in the country for inspection, reopening only the solvent ones under Treasury oversight, a pause that stopped the panic almost immediately.

Over the following hundred days Congress passed programme after programme: the Civilian Conservation Corps put young men to work planting trees and building trails, the Agricultural Adjustment Administration paid farmers to cut production and raise prices, and the Tennessee Valley Authority began wiring electricity into a region that had gone without it. The pace of that spring gave the whole decade of legislation that followed its name.

Nixon had built his career on hard anti-communism, which made him an unlikely candidate to fly to Beijing. He arrived on 21 February 1972 for a week of talks with Mao Zedong and Premier Zhou Enlai, ending twenty-three years in which Washington and the People's Republic had had almost no direct contact.

The visit produced the Shanghai Communique on 27 February, a statement in which both sides acknowledged deep differences, particularly over Taiwan, while agreeing to work toward normal relations. Full diplomatic recognition did not follow until 1979; what the trip achieved in 1972 was simply reopening a conversation that had been closed since 1949.

Leaders gathered in Belgrade on 1 September 1961 for the first Conference of Heads of State or Government of Non-Aligned Countries, drawing on principles the Bandung Conference had set out six years earlier. Yugoslavia's Josip Broz Tito hosted; Egypt's Nasser, India's Nehru, Ghana's Nkrumah and Indonesia's Sukarno were among the leaders who shaped the founding agenda.

None of the five had any interest in taking orders from Washington or Moscow, and Tito in particular used the movement to keep Yugoslavia's communism independent of Soviet control. The movement never became a formal bloc with binding rules, but it gave dozens of newly independent states a shared platform for arguing against alignment with either Cold War superpower.

Only five states had tested nuclear weapons when the treaty opened for signature in 1968, and the deal it offered was uneven by design. Recognised nuclear powers kept their arsenals for now; everyone else promised not to acquire any, in exchange for help with peaceful nuclear technology and eventual disarmament talks.

It entered into force on 5 March 1970 and now binds 191 states, more than almost any other arms agreement. India, Pakistan, Israel and, later, North Korea never accepted its terms or withdrew from them, and each went on to build a nuclear arsenal outside the treaty's reach.

Delegates from Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela met in Baghdad from 10 to 14 September 1960 and agreed to found the organisation on the final day. The trigger was blunt: multinational oil companies had cut the posted price of crude in 1959 and again that August, without asking the countries the oil came from.

The five founders were answering a market dominated by a handful of Western firms known as the Seven Sisters, who set prices largely on their own terms. OPEC's early role was coordination rather than control; it took over a decade, and several more members joining, before it could move prices by acting together rather than merely comparing notes.

Osman I did not inherit an empire. He led a small band of Turkic warriors, the Kayi, in a border region of northwestern Anatolia that his father Ertugrul had held before him, and for years his ambitions ran to capturing individual fortress towns from Byzantine garrisons rather than founding a dynasty. His victory at Bapheus in 1302 was the beylik's first major win against Byzantine forces.

Osman never took Bursa, the city that became his son Orhan's capital in 1326, and he was dead by the time it fell. What he left behind was a working state with its own administration and a reputation for alliances that crossed religious lines, foundations solid enough that his descendants built an empire on them that lasted into the twentieth century.

The papacy needed rescuing before it could be granted anything. When the Lombards seized the Byzantine-held Exarchate of Ravenna in 751, the Duchy of Rome was cut off from Constantinople with no army of its own to call on, leaving Pope Stephen II to look for protection elsewhere.

He found it in Pepin, the Frankish king whom Stephen's predecessor had already crowned in place of the powerless Merovingian line. Pepin marched into Italy, defeated the Lombards, and in 756 handed the former Ravenna territories to the pope rather than keeping them for himself, a grant that gave the papacy direct rule over central Italian land for the next eleven centuries.

Four parties signed in Paris on 27 January 1973: the United States, North Vietnam, South Vietnam and the Provisional Revolutionary Government representing the Viet Cong. The deal set a ceasefire, required American forces out within sixty days, and allowed prisoner exchanges, but it also let North Vietnamese troops already in the South stay where they were.

That last concession undid the rest. Both sides broke the ceasefire almost immediately, and by March 1973 fighting had resumed in full. Washington did not intervene again; North Vietnamese forces expanded their hold over the next two years and took Saigon in April 1975, ending the war the accords had claimed to settle.

Poland-Lithuania had no army capable of stopping what came next. After the Bar Confederation's rebels lost their fight against Russian influence, Russia, Prussia and Austria simply agreed among themselves to take slices of the commonwealth rather than let any one of them seize it all. Poland's own diet was left to ratify losses it had no power to refuse.

Prussia took Royal Prussia and land along the Notec river, Austria took Galicia along with the salt mines at Bochnia and Wieliczka, and Russia took Polish Livonia and part of eastern Lithuania. Between them the three powers took roughly 30 percent of the commonwealth's territory and about half its population, a first cut that two further partitions would finish within twenty-three years.

Peace is a generous word for it. Augustus's own reign still saw wars on the Rhine and in Spain and the destruction of three legions in Germany's Teutoburg Forest in 9 CE. What the Pax Romana meant in practice was the end of the civil wars that had torn the Mediterranean apart for a century, not an absence of fighting at the empire's edges.

Inside those edges, though, trade moved with unusual freedom: roads, a common currency and a single legal system connected Britain to Egypt without a border crossing between them. Historians generally count the peace as lasting until Marcus Aurelius's reign in the late second century, roughly two hundred years in which no rival claimant tore Rome itself apart.

The settlement of 1555 ran on a single principle, cuius regio, eius religio: whichever faith a prince held became the official religion of his territory, and subjects who could not accept it were free to leave with their property rather than face persecution. It ended years of armed standoff between Charles V and the Lutheran princes without either side conceding the theological argument.

It protected exactly two churches. Article 17 shut out everyone else by name, so Calvinists, Zwinglians and Anabaptists gained no legal standing at all and remained open to punishment. That gap stayed unresolved for almost a century, until the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 finally extended recognition to Calvinism.

Signed in April 1559, the treaty closed six decades of intermittent war between France and Spain over Italy. France gave up its claims to Naples, Sicily and Milan and pulled out of Piedmont, while Spain handed back the northern French fortresses it had taken at Saint-Quentin and elsewhere. France kept Calais, seized from England the year before, and the Three Bishoprics of Toul, Metz and Verdun.

The peace was sealed with two royal marriages, and it was the wedding celebrations that killed a king. Jousting in Paris that July, Henry II took a splintered lance through the eye from Gabriel de Montgomery and died ten days later, leaving France under a fifteen-year-old and heading into decades of religious civil war.

The sticking point was money. France agreed to drop its support for Portugal and gave up its claim to Catalonia, while Spain ceded Roussillon and Artois and handed over a string of Flanders towns including Arras and Gravelines. The border it drew still runs along the crest of the Pyrenees, with one accidental gap: no one specified which side of a ridge Llivia sat on, so it stayed Spanish, an enclave inside French territory.

The peace was sealed by marrying Louis XIV to Maria Theresa, daughter of Philip IV of Spain, who renounced her claim to the Spanish throne in return for a dowry. Spain never paid it.
