Louis later cited the missing dowry as grounds to invade the Spanish Netherlands, launching the War of Devolution in 1667.

Winston Churchill did not see the conference through. He arrived on 17 July 1945, left mid-talks to await the results of a British election, and returned to learn he had lost. Clement Attlee took his seat at the table for the final week, with Ernest Bevin as his new foreign secretary, while Stalin and Truman remained the whole time.

Truman used the meeting to tell Stalin, obliquely, that the United States had a powerful new weapon. Stalin, who already knew of the atomic bomb through Soviet espionage, showed little reaction and said he hoped it would be used against Japan. The three delegations also fixed Germany's occupation zones and moved its eastern border to the Oder-Neisse line.

The Volstead Act defined any drink over half a percent alcohol as illegal, and it came into force at one minute past midnight on 17 January 1920. Enforcement started immediately: in New York a Brooklyn cafe owner was arrested for selling brandy just four minutes into the new law, and Indianapolis made an arrest within five.

Around 1,520 federal agents were assigned to police the entire country, a force too small to stop the bootlegging and speakeasies that followed within months. The law banned manufacturing and selling alcohol but never made drinking itself a crime, a gap that shaped how the following thirteen years played out.

Twenty-three years of fighting over Sicily ended not on a battlefield but at the negotiating table, once Carthage's fleet had been broken and the island's cities had run out of reasons to keep resisting. The Treaty of Lutatius in 241 BCE forced Carthage out of Sicily entirely, handed Rome all prisoners, and set an indemnity of 3,200 talents of silver, payable over ten years.

Rome was not finished squeezing afterward. A few years later, while Carthage was distracted putting down a mercenary revolt, Rome demanded Sardinia and Corsica as well, along with another 1,200 talents, and Carthage gave way rather than fight a war it could not yet afford. The resentment this left behind fed directly into the far larger war that began in 218 BCE.

King Zheng of Qin spent nine years finishing what generations of Warring States rivals had failed to do. Han fell in 230 BCE, then Zhao, Wei, Chu and Yan in turn, and by 221 BCE the last holdout, Qi, had surrendered. Zheng took a new title, Qin Shi Huang, first emperor, rather than remaining just another king among equals.

Conquest was the easy part; holding the result together was the project that followed. With his minister Li Si, he forced the former rival states onto one script, one currency, the Ban Liang coin, and standard weights and measures, even fixing the width of wagon axles so carts built anywhere could use the same roads. The empire he built lasted barely fifteen years after his death, but the administrative unity outlived it.

Beijing fell twice in two months in 1644. Rebel forces took it in April and the last Ming emperor, Chongzhen, hanged himself rather than be captured. The Manchu regent Dorgon then allied with the Ming general Wu Sangui, who had been guarding the Shanhai Pass and turned against the rebels after they seized his father and his household.

Wu and Dorgon crushed the rebel army at Shanhai Pass in May and marched into Beijing days later. Rather than present themselves as conquerors, the Manchus held a formal funeral for Chongzhen and styled themselves heirs to the fallen Ming, a claim to legitimacy that eased the takeover of a much larger population by a much smaller one.

Henry Dunant was a Swiss businessman travelling to see Napoleon III on unrelated matters when he arrived at Solferino in northern Italy on 24 June 1859, the day of the battle, and found some 40,000 wounded and dying men with almost no medical care between them. He organised local villagers to tend soldiers of both sides under the motto tutti fratelli, all are brothers, and wrote up the experience in a short book, A Memory of Solferino.

That book reached the Geneva Society for Public Welfare, which on 9 February 1863 approved Dunant's proposal for a permanent relief organisation. A five-member committee held its first meeting on 17 February 1863, the date now treated as the founding of what became the International Committee of the Red Cross.

Deng Xiaoping had no formal title as head of state or government when he set China on a new economic course at the Third Plenum of the Eleventh Central Committee on 18 December 1978. He used his standing within the party to steer it away from Maoist collectivism without ever holding the top job himself.

Farmers were allowed to sell surplus produce after meeting state quotas under what became known as the household responsibility system, and coastal cities such as Shenzhen were opened as special zones offering tax breaks to foreign investors. Agricultural output rose sharply through the following decade as the changes spread beyond their original testing grounds.

On 7 March 1936, German troops crossed into the Rhineland, a strip of their own territory that Versailles and then Locarno had bound Germany to keep free of soldiers and fortifications. France's general staff had the stronger army on paper but told the government that pushing the Germans back out would mean full mobilisation, at a cost officials judged the treasury could not bear.

Britain's cabinet took the same view, one official noting a Commons mood so sympathetic to the German case that few there wanted to risk war over it. Neither government moved beyond a diplomatic protest, and William Shirer later described this moment as the last point at which Western Europe could have stopped Hitler's rearmament cheaply.

Octavian did not call himself king or emperor. After beating Mark Antony at Actium in 31 BCE and taking Egypt, he handed his extraordinary powers back to the Senate in 27 BCE, in a staged gesture the Senate answered by handing most of them straight back, along with a new name: Augustus, the revered one.

He kept the tribune's powers, control of the army and most of the provinces, while consuls and the Senate carried on meeting as if the Republic still ran itself. That fiction, government dressed as restoration, is what historians call the principate, and it is the arrangement that later emperors inherited rather than a single dramatic coronation.

The story Romans told themselves is a rape and a suicide. Sextus Tarquinius, son of the king Tarquin the Proud, assaulted a noblewoman named Lucretia, who killed herself after naming her attacker. Her kinsman Lucius Junius Brutus is said to have raised Rome against the monarchy in response, expelling the king in 509 BCE.

Most modern historians treat that account as legend layered over a much less dramatic event, probably an aristocratic power shift within Tarquin's own family, or the end of an Etruscan occupation of the city. What followed is better attested: royal power passed to two consuls elected annually, each able to veto the other, a structure meant to prevent any one man from ruling as king again.

Talks that began in Helsinki in November 1969 dragged on for two and a half years before Richard Nixon and Leonid Brezhnev signed anything in Moscow. What they produced on 26 May 1972 was less a disarmament deal than a freeze: existing numbers of strategic missile launchers were locked in place rather than reduced.

A linked Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty, signed the same day, limited each side to two missile defence sites, later cut to one. SALT I did not touch bomber fleets or the accuracy of warheads, and both sides kept building within its limits, but it was the first agreement in which Washington and Moscow accepted outside constraints on their nuclear arsenals at all.

Jimmy Carter and Leonid Brezhnev signed SALT II in Vienna's Hofburg Palace on 18 June 1979, extending the limits their predecessors had agreed on missile launchers into a fuller cap on delivery vehicles and warheads. It was meant to buy time for a more ambitious follow-up treaty.

That follow-up never came. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan that December, and the discovery of a Soviet brigade in Cuba, killed any chance of Senate ratification, and Carter withdrew the treaty from consideration in January 1980. Neither side ever ratified it, yet both largely kept to its limits until it lapsed at the end of 1985.

Eight countries signed the Southeast Asia Collective Defense Treaty in Manila on 8 September 1954: Australia, France, New Zealand, Pakistan, the Philippines, Thailand, the United Kingdom and the United States. Only two of the eight, Thailand and the Philippines, were themselves in Southeast Asia. Its headquarters opened in Bangkok the following February.

SEATO never built the joint command NATO had. Pakistan quit in 1973 after losing its eastern half to Bangladesh, France stopped paying its share in 1975, and South Vietnam, which the treaty had been built to protect, fell that same year. The organisation held a last military exercise in February 1976 and dissolved in June 1977.

Singapore had joined the Federation of Malaysia only in 1963, and the merger did not settle much. Trade disputes, disagreements over race-based policy and communal riots in 1964 left the two governments barely on speaking terms within two years of union.

Secret talks between Kuala Lumpur and Singapore produced a separation agreement, and on 9 August 1965 the Malaysian Parliament voted 126 to 0 to let Singapore go. Lee Kuan Yew, who had campaigned for merger, became prime minister of a country he had not sought, with no natural resources and a population he once doubted could survive alone.

Roosevelt signed the Social Security Act on 14 August 1935, creating a federal pension funded by a payroll tax on current workers rather than by savings each person had set aside. Alongside old-age benefits it set up state-run unemployment insurance and aid for families headed by a single mother, the first time the federal government had underwritten either.

The original law left large groups out: farm labourers, domestic servants and most government employees were not covered, a gap that fell hardest on Black workers in the rural South, where a majority of them worked in excluded jobs. Congress extended coverage to most of these groups only in later decades.

Zhao Kuangyin did not seize power through open rebellion but through a staged mutiny. His own soldiers, the story goes, draped a yellow robe over him at Chenqiao in 960 and refused to march further under anyone else, forcing the boy emperor of the Later Zhou to abdicate in his favour. He took the name Taizu and spent sixteen years subduing the remaining kingdoms to reunify China.

The dynasty he founded is remembered less for its army than for what it printed, financed and built. Song China issued the world's first paper banknotes, developed movable type printing, fitted ships with a compass for true north, and fielded gunpowder weapons including fire lances, all inside a state that also recruited its officials through competitive written examinations.

Before 1710, printing rights in England belonged to the Stationers' Company, a guild that had held a near-permanent monopoly on what could legally be published since the previous century. The Statute of Anne broke that hold by putting copyright into law for the first time and, crucially, giving it to authors rather than the printers who set their type.

The term was modest by later standards: fourteen years from publication, with a second fourteen-year renewal if the author was still alive when it expired. Works already in print got twenty-one years. Once the clock ran out, the text became free for anyone to print, a deliberate limit that later copyright law kept extending but never dropped.

Before 1931, an act passed at Westminster could bind Canada, Australia or the other dominions whether or not their own parliaments agreed to it. The Statute of Westminster ended that: it barred any future UK law from applying to a dominion unless that dominion had asked for it, turning a legal hierarchy into a group of equals bound only by shared allegiance to the Crown.

Canada, the Irish Free State and South Africa took the statute's effect immediately in 1931; Australia, New Zealand and Newfoundland delayed formal adoption for years afterward. It followed directly from the Balfour Declaration of 1926, in which Britain and the dominions had already agreed, in principle, that none stood subordinate to another.

Sudan had been ruled since 1899 as an Anglo-Egyptian condominium, nominally shared between Cairo and London but administered in practice much like a British colony. That arrangement began to unravel after Egypt's 1952 revolution, whose leaders, including the half-Sudanese Muhammad Naguib, pressed for British withdrawal from both Egypt and Sudan.

Sudan became fully independent on 1 January 1956, ending both British and Egyptian authority at once rather than transferring power from one to the other. A parliamentary government took office in Khartoum, though the new state inherited a divide between the Arab-majority north and the south that would erupt into civil war within months.

The document dated 1291 says nothing about crossbows or apples. It is a defensive pact among three valley communities, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden, promising mutual help and a peaceful way to settle disputes among themselves, mainly to keep their mountain trade routes free of outside interference. The famous oath on the Rutli meadow, tied to the William Tell story, is a later tradition, dated by a sixteenth century chronicler to 1307.

The three Forest communities fought off a Habsburg army in 1315 and pledged, from then on, not to make outside alliances without each other's consent. Other valleys and cities joined over the following centuries, and the loose alliance that grew from this original charter became modern Switzerland, which still marks 1291 as its founding date.

Li Yuan did not plan a dynasty so much as survive one collapsing around him. As a Sui official and cousin of the reigning emperor, he watched Sui rule disintegrate into revolt, and in 618, after Emperor Yang was murdered by his own officers, Li Yuan declared himself emperor rather than wait to be swept away with the regime he had served.

His rebellion had an unusual figure at its edge: his daughter, Princess Pingyang, who raised and personally commanded her own troops during the fighting. Once established, the dynasty's second ruler, Li Shimin, pushed Tang territory past the old Han borders and drew up a legal code that Chinese dynasties kept copying for centuries.

The Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and the United States signed the treaty in Moscow on 5 August 1963, less than a year after the Cuban Missile Crisis had shown how close the two superpowers could come to disaster. It took effect that October and well over a hundred further countries eventually joined it.

Negotiators had originally hoped for a complete ban but gave up on covering underground tests, since verifying them without intrusive inspections proved technically hard and politically unwelcome to Moscow. What the treaty did stop was atmospheric, underwater and space detonations, ending the practice of venting fallout directly into the air that people breathed.

Nobody had organised Roman law in over a century when Theodosius II ordered the job done in 429. Imperial rulings since Constantine's reign, more than 2,500 of them scattered across a hundred years of edicts, letters and rescripts, were gathered, sorted by subject and stripped of anything obsolete or contradictory.

The finished code was published in February 438 and took effect across both halves of the empire, east and west, on the first day of the following January, with Valentinian III agreeing to enforce it in Ravenna as well as Constantinople. It gave later compilers, including Justinian a century afterward, a model to build on rather than start from scratch.

Tokugawa Ieyasu had already won the decisive battle three years earlier at Sekigahara, ending a century of civil war among Japan's regional lords. In 1603 he took the title of shogun and ruled from Edo Castle, in what is now Tokyo, leaving the emperor in Kyoto as a figurehead while real authority sat with him and the daimyo who answered to him.

The isolation the shogunate became known for took decades to close in fully. Ieyasu banned Catholicism outright in 1614, and by 1635 his successors barred Japanese subjects from leaving the country and shut the ports to everyone but China, Korea and the Dutch, a policy that held with little change until the mid-1800s.

Britain handed the French fortress of Louisbourg back to France in exchange for Madras, a trading post in India that a French fleet had captured three years earlier. British and American colonists who had bled to take Louisbourg were furious to see a European negotiator swap it for a foothold on another continent entirely.

Every major power signed the 1748 settlement and almost none of them liked it. Maria Theresa got her succession as Habsburg ruler confirmed but resented losing Silesia to Prussia in the bargain, Spain thought its gains too small, and France's own public called the peace as bad as the war it ended. Most parties treated it as a pause rather than a resolution, and fighting resumed within eight years.

Castile and Portugal signed the Treaty of Alcacovas on 4 September 1479 to end a war neither side had clearly won. Castile's forces, backed by Ferdinand and Isabella, had the upper hand on land, while Portugal's fleets controlled the sea, so the settlement split the difference: the rival claimant to Castile's throne renounced her claim, and a royal marriage sealed the peace.

Buried in the same treaty was a division of the Atlantic that would matter more than the war itself. Castile kept the Canary Islands, while Portugal secured Madeira, the Azores, Cape Verde and the West African coast, along with exclusive rights to sail and trade anywhere in the ocean south of the Canaries. Thirteen years before Columbus sailed, the two crowns had already agreed how to carve up an Atlantic neither had explored.

The 1667 settlement between England and the Dutch Republic was less a negotiation than a bookkeeping exercise. The two sides agreed on uti possidetis, a principle that each kept whatever it currently held on the ground, with an effective date set for 20 May of that year. It was a quick way to end a war neither side was winning outright.

Under that rule, the Dutch kept Suriname, a South American sugar colony, and the nutmeg island of Run, while England kept New Netherland, seized from the Dutch two years earlier and already renamed New York after the king's brother. At the time, the nutmeg island looked like the better prize.

Robert Cecil led the English delegation that met Spanish and Habsburg envoys in London in 1604, closing a war that had run since 1585 without either side ever forcing a decision. Elizabeth I, who had backed the fight for two decades, had died the year before, and her successor James I had little appetite for continuing it.

The peace restored the position each side had held before the fighting started. Spain accepted James's Protestant crown and dropped any plan to restore Catholicism in England; England, in turn, stopped funding the Dutch rebels and English ships stopped raiding Spanish shipping in the Atlantic. Spain also agreed to end its military involvement in Ireland.

Francis I had been captured at the Battle of Pavia in 1525 and held in Spain for almost a year before he would agree to terms. The treaty he signed in Madrid in January 1526 gave up his claims to Burgundy, Flanders, Artois and Italy, and left his two young sons behind as hostages against his word.

His word did not last long. Within weeks of returning to France he repudiated the treaty, arguing he had signed it only under duress as a prisoner, and formed the League of Cognac against Charles V instead. Burgundy stayed French; the war over Italy dragged on for years more.

The agreement was signed aboard the British warship HMS Cornwallis, anchored off Nanjing, on 29 August 1842. It closed the First Opium War, fought after Chinese officials destroyed British-owned opium stocks at Canton, and it was written entirely on British terms.

Beyond handing over Hong Kong, the treaty forced open four more ports, Xiamen, Fuzhou, Ningbo and Shanghai, to foreign trade, and required 27 million silver dollars, covering the destroyed opium, the 1841 ransom of Canton, merchant debts and British war costs. It was the first of what China would later call the unequal treaties, a term that stuck to the whole series that followed it.

Nijmegen was not one treaty but a sequence signed by exhausted parties between 1678 and 1679, closing out the Franco-Dutch War: France and the Dutch Republic first, then France and Spain, then settlements with Brandenburg, Sweden, Denmark and the Holy Roman Empire trailing behind. Louis XIV negotiated separately with each so that no ally could hold up his terms with the others.

France gave up Maastricht and the Principality of Orange to William of Orange, but took Franche-Comte outright from Spain along with a run of Flanders and Hainaut towns, including Ypres, Cassel and Valenciennes. The new French border it left behind sat close to where the modern frontier with Belgium still runs.

France gave up nearly all of its North American mainland claims in 1763, ceding Canada and the land east of the Mississippi to Britain outright. West of the river, Louisiana had already gone to Spain in a separate, secret handover the year before, so France left the continent with almost nothing.

Britain gave some of it back elsewhere: it returned Guadeloupe, Martinique and Saint Lucia to France, and Havana and Manila, both seized during the war, to Spain. Britain kept Canada and Florida rather than the Caribbean sugar islands, a choice that looked odd to contemporaries who valued sugar revenue over cold farmland.

Delegates signed the treaty in Rome's Palazzo dei Conservatori on 25 March 1957. Belgium, France, West Germany, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands were the six governments involved, the same six that had already pooled their coal and steel industries earlier in the decade. The treaty took effect on the first day of 1958.

What it created was a common market rather than a currency or a parliament with real teeth: internal tariffs would fall over a transition period and a shared external tariff would rise in their place. That body, the European Economic Community, absorbed Euratom's founding treaty on the same day and later grew into the European Union, expanding well beyond its original six members.

Nobody at Ryswick expected the peace to hold. The 1697 settlement closing the Nine Years' War mostly put Europe back where it had stood before the fighting started: France handed back Lorraine, Freiburg and Breisach, and pulled its troops out of Catalonia and several towns in the Spanish Netherlands, while keeping Strasbourg.

Louis XIV also recognised William III as King of England, dropped his support for the exiled Stuart claimant, and gave up rival claims on two German electorates. Both sides treated the deal as a pause rather than a resolution, watching the childless King Charles II of Spain, and war over his succession broke out again within three years of his death in 1700.

The line agreed at Tordesillas ran 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands, roughly 2,100 kilometres of open Atlantic with almost nothing charted on either side of it. Everything discovered to the east went to Portugal, everything to the west to Castile, drawn up by Ferdinand and Isabella and John II of Portugal without asking Pope Alexander VI, whose earlier bulls it quietly overrode.

Nobody else in Europe felt bound by it. France's king Francis I is said to have asked to see the clause in Adam's will that excluded him from the world, and England and the Dutch, being Protestant, saw no reason to honour a line brokered by the Pope between two Catholic crowns. It took Julius II until 1506 to bless the treaty at all.

The treaties signed at Utrecht in 1713 let Philip V keep the Spanish throne on one condition: he and his heirs gave up any claim to France, and French princes gave up any claim to Spain, so the same king could never rule both. That single renunciation was the point the other terms were built around.

Britain came away the best paid party in the room. Spain ceded Gibraltar and Menorca, France handed over Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and Hudson Bay territory in North America, and Britain won a thirty-year contract, the asiento, to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish American colonies, a monopoly France had held until then.

Three brothers spent three years fighting each other before agreeing to stop. Lothair, Louis and Charles, all grandsons of Charlemagne, had already gone to war over their father Louis the Pious's uneven attempts to divide the inheritance, and only after Lothair's defeat at Fontenoy in 841 did the brothers sit down to settle it in 843.

The line they drew ran a middle kingdom, Lothair's Francia Media, between an eastern realm for Louis and a western one for Charles. The middle strip did not last: it splintered within a generation, while the eastern and western portions held together long enough to become the rough outlines of Germany and France.

At Waitangi in the Bay of Islands on 6 February 1840, around forty Maori chiefs put their names or marks to an agreement with the British Crown, with more signing at further sites over the following months. The document exists in two texts, English and Maori, drafted in haste and not identical in meaning.

Where the English version ceded the chiefs' sovereignty outright, the Maori text spoke of kawanatanga, closer to governance than sovereignty, while a promise of continued rangatiratanga over land and possessions left chiefs believing they retained authority the English wording did not grant them. That gap between the two texts has shaped New Zealand law and politics ever since.

Guthrum came to terms with Alfred only after losing a battle, not a war of attrition. His Viking army had chased Alfred into hiding in the Somerset marshes over the winter of 878, but Alfred's forces defeated Guthrum decisively at Ethandun that spring, and the peace struck afterward, remembered as the Treaty of Wedmore, was Guthrum's price for keeping his life.

Its terms were narrower than later legend suggests: Guthrum agreed to be baptised, taking Alfred as his godfather, and to withdraw his army from Wessex. The formal border between English and Viking-held territory, the line that created the Danelaw, was settled separately in a later, written agreement between the two leaders.

Italy signed on 20 May 1882 chiefly out of anger at France, which had just taken Tunisia, territory Italy had wanted for itself. Germany and Austria-Hungary already had a defensive pact of their own and extended it to include Italy, promising to back Rome if France attacked first, while Italy pledged neutrality if Russia moved against Vienna.

The alliance was renewed every few years into the twentieth century, but it depended on Austria-Hungary being the one attacked, not the aggressor. When Vienna itself opened hostilities in 1914, Italy declared neutrality and, the following year, joined the opposing side instead, ending its part in the pact for good.

No single document created the Triple Entente. It grew from three separate deals: a Franco-Russian alliance from 1894, the Anglo-French Entente Cordiale of 1904, and the 1907 Anglo-Russian Convention, which settled British and Russian rivalry over Persia, Afghanistan and Tibet by dividing Persia into zones of influence.

A British official, Eyre Crowe, called the resulting arrangement between the three powers little more than a shared frame of mind rather than a binding pact, and it carried no mutual defence obligation. That looseness let Britain weigh its own response independently in 1914, even though France, Russia and Britain all ended up fighting the Central Powers together.

Before 450 BCE, Roman law lived in the memories of patrician priests, who could tell plebeians whatever they liked and call it tradition. Plebeians pushed back the one way that worked: secessio, walking out of the city en masse and leaving Rome without its labourers and soldiers until the Senate agreed to write the law down.

A board of ten men, the decemviri, drafted ten tables in 450 BCE and two more the following year, reportedly after sending someone to study Greek law codes first. The finished text was cast in bronze and set up in the Forum where anyone could read it. Much of the content covered everyday disputes, debt, property, family, but the act of posting it at all was the point: the law could no longer be whatever a patrician said it was that day.

Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan did not inherit the caliphate so much as outlast his rivals for it. As governor of Syria, he refused to accept Ali as caliph after the murder of Uthman, and years of civil war between their factions, the First Fitna, ended only when Ali was assassinated in 661 and Mu'awiya's forces held the field.

He moved the capital and treasury from Medina to Damascus, his own long-held power base, turning what had been an Arabian institution into one governed from a Roman-Byzantine city. He also broke with precedent by naming his own son as successor, making the caliphate hereditary for the first time.

Queen Margaret I of Denmark built the Union of Kalmar around a boy who was not her son. Eric of Pomerania, her adopted great nephew, had no personal claim strong enough to unite three kingdoms on his own, so it was Margaret's own standing as regent of Denmark, Norway and already much of Sweden that made his coronation at Kalmar on 17 June 1397 possible.

The three crowns stayed nominally joined for over a century, but Denmark was never quite strong enough to hold Norway and Sweden inside it against their own nobles' wishes. Resentment of Danish dominance ran especially deep in Sweden, and after the Stockholm Bloodbath of 1520 a rebellion led by Gustav Vasa broke the union for good when he was elected King of Sweden in 1523.

The Union of Krewo was a marriage contract before it was anything else. Jogaila, Grand Duke of Lithuania, agreed to marry the young Queen Jadwiga of Poland, and to pay 200,000 florins to buy her out of an existing engagement to a Habsburg duke. In return he became King of Poland the following year, ruling by right of his wife rather than by his own crown.

The price was religious. Jogaila had to convert from paganism to Catholicism and take the baptismal name Wladyslaw, then bring the Lithuanian nobility with him and free tens of thousands of Polish captives held from earlier wars. The union bound two states that had spent generations fighting each other into a partnership that, through later treaties, lasted for four centuries.

Signed on 23 January 1579, the Union bound Holland, Zeeland, Utrecht and Groningen together on shared defence, taxation and, unusually for the time, a promise of personal freedom of religion. It answered the Union of Arras, signed weeks earlier, in which the southern provinces had reaffirmed their loyalty to Philip II and split the Low Countries along a line still visible in the Belgian-Dutch border.

More provinces joined through 1579 and 1580, among them Ghent, Antwerp and Brussels, though Upper Guelders never signed at all. The agreement made no claim to independence itself, but it gave the northern provinces a shared structure to govern themselves with, one historians treat as the working foundation of the republic they later became.

Delegates from fifty governments met in San Francisco starting 25 April 1945, while fighting in Europe was still going on, to turn the wartime alliance into a permanent body. Two months of drafting produced a charter signed on 26 June 1945; Poland, absent from the conference, added its signature later and is still counted among the founding members.

The charter took legal effect on 24 October 1945 once the five states meant to hold permanent Security Council seats, along with a majority of the other signatories, had ratified it. That date is marked each year as United Nations Day, distinct from the June signing that most accounts point to as the founding moment.

Nine states had to say yes before the document drafted in Philadelphia could take effect, and nobody was certain they would. Delaware ratified first, in December 1787. New Hampshire became the ninth in June 1788, clearing the threshold, though the outcome had been anything but settled in several state conventions where the vote was close and bitterly argued.

New York and Virginia, whose support the new government badly needed, ratified only after Federalist writers, chiefly Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay, published a long series of newspaper essays defending the plan. Both states came around only once opponents were promised that a bill of rights would follow. It did, four years later.

The treaty signed in Washington on 19 January 1960 replaced a 1951 security pact that Japan had accepted as the price of ending American occupation. The new version added mutual defence obligations and required Washington to consult Tokyo before moving forces, terms the original had not bothered to include.

Ratifying it back in Japan proved far harder than negotiating it. Prime Minister Nobusuke Kishi forced a vote through parliament after having police carry out Socialist lawmakers who tried to block it, and the manoeuvre triggered some of the largest protests in Japan's postwar history. A Tokyo University student, Michiko Kanba, died in clashes near parliament on 15 June, days before the treaty took effect.

Four republics signed the treaty of union on 30 December 1922: Russia, Ukraine, Byelorussia and the Transcaucasian Federation, which then covered Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan together. Mikhail Kalinin led the Russian delegation, and the document was ratified the next day by the first Congress of Soviets.

The new union kept the outward form of a federation of sovereign states, each with its own government and, on paper, a right to secede. In practice power ran through the Communist Party rather than through those republican structures, and further republics joined the union over the following decades as Soviet borders shifted.

On 7 March 1965, state troopers attacked civil rights marchers crossing the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama, with tear gas and clubs. Televised images of the assault, later called Bloody Sunday, pushed Congress toward action that had stalled for years despite the Fifteenth Amendment's fifty-year-old promise.

President Lyndon Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act on 6 August 1965. It outlawed literacy tests and similar devices used to disqualify Black voters, and it required jurisdictions with a documented history of discrimination to clear any change to voting rules with federal officials before enacting it.

Moscow signed the treaty on 14 May 1955, five days after West Germany formally joined NATO. Seven other governments put their names to it alongside the Soviet Union: Albania, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, East Germany, Hungary, Poland and Romania. The stated purpose was collective security in Europe, but the timing tied it directly to West German rearmament.

In practice the pact's forces were used against its own members more often than against NATO. Soviet-led troops crushed the Hungarian uprising in 1956 and, under the pact's banner, invaded Czechoslovakia in 1968 to end the Prague Spring. Albania withdrew in 1968 in protest at that invasion, and the alliance itself dissolved in 1991 as Soviet control over Eastern Europe collapsed.

Five countries, the United States, Britain, Japan, France and Italy, agreed in 1922 to hold their battleship tonnage to a fixed ratio near 5:5:3:1.75:1.75, letting the US and Britain each keep 525,000 tons of capital ships while Japan was held to 315,000. Individual battleships were capped at 35,000 tons and guns no larger than 16 inches.

Cruisers, destroyers and submarines were left uncapped in number, only in size, at 10,000 tons apiece, a gap navies spent the following decade exploiting. Japan resented a ratio that ranked it below Britain and the United States, and the treaty's limits held only until the 1930s, when Japan withdrew from them.

Tennessee's ratification on 18 August 1920 was the 36th needed to put the amendment into the Constitution, and it came down to one vote. Harry Burn, a 24 year old state representative who had opposed ratification, switched sides on the floor after his mother mailed him a note telling him to vote for suffrage.

Opponents tried to stop a final quorum by fleeing across the state line to Decatur, Alabama, but the tally already stood. A suffragist in the chamber rang a small Liberty Bell replica when the result was confirmed, and the amendment was certified on 26 August 1920.

Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin spent eight days in February 1945 at palaces on the Crimean coast near Yalta, meeting while Soviet troops were already inside Germany. They agreed to split Germany and Berlin into occupation zones, with France given a zone carved from the American and British shares, and to move Poland's eastern border to the Curzon Line while compensating Poland with German territory in the west.

Stalin promised to enter the war against Japan within three months of Germany's surrender, in exchange for territory including South Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands, and agreed the Soviet Union would join the new United Nations with a Security Council veto. The three also signed a declaration promising free elections across liberated Europe, a promise Stalin did not keep in the territories his army occupied.
